question: EUR 200 billion for Global Europe, EUR 100 billion for Ukraine. And at home, new levies on businesses and households

In the next seven-year budget, the Commission wants to allocate EUR 200 billion to the Global Europe instrument. This is intended to fund assistance to countries outside the Union, support for accession candidates and foreign projects such as Global Gateway. On top of that, EUR 15 billion is to go into a reserve. Separately, outside this budget framework, it is proposing up to another EUR 100 billion for Ukraine.

Altogether, this amounts to hundreds of billions of euros that will flow out of the EU. At the same time, the Commission says there is not enough money for matters within the Union and is demanding new levies from businesses and citizens. 1.
Why does the Commission say that there is not enough money in the Union while at the same time sending hundreds of billions beyond its borders?
Why, according to the Commission, should taxpayers in the Member States pay for this when public resources in Europe are supposedly insufficient even for domestic priorities?
Why is the Commission seeking new levies instead of significantly cutting expenditure outside the Union?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.10.2026) External action and internal EU policies are not competing priorities but complementary investments in a stable and prosperous EU. In the current global context, the EU can no longer afford growing exposure to external shocks.

Investing in the stability of its neighbourhood, addressing migration at its source and securing market access amid rising global competition is not optional – it reflects the EU’s ambition to be a reliable partner and it generates tangible returns for EU businesses and citizens through trade, access to critical resources and stronger partnerships.

The 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework proposal is designed to complement Member States’ budgets and deliver results that national budgets cannot achieve alone. For Ukraine and for activities funded by Global Europe1, the EU budget prevents the duplication of efforts and resources among Member States.

Hence, the EU budget contributes to more cost-effective spending on external policy, creating space for other policies in national budgets. Furthermore, the EU faces growing demands in areas such as competitiveness, defence, and climate action; while support for long-standing policies such as cohesion and the common agricultural policy remains essential.

Introducing new own resources would diversify revenue streams, reduce the burden on Member States’ national budgets and ensure the sustainable funding of common EU policies, and financing the repayment of NextGenerationEU borrowing due to begin in 20282.
